hints: Start from the atomic number of Zn (30) and write the full atom configuration first, then think about which electrons are lost to form Zn2+.
walkthrough:
Remember how Zn loses electrons**
Zinc as an atom is $[\text{Ar}]$ $3\text{d}^{10}4\text{s}^{2}$. A very common slip is to take electrons from the 3d first. Always remove the $4\text{s}$ electrons first because they are the outermost shell, even though 4s fills before 3d when building up.

Fill the boxes correctly**
Removing two $4\text{s}$ electrons leaves $3\text{d}^{10}$. That means each of the five 3d boxes gets two arrows, one up and one down. Leave the single 4s box and the three 4p boxes completely empty.
Final answer: $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]$ $3\text{d}^{10}$: all five 3d boxes fully filled with paired arrows (up and down), 4s box empty, all three 4p boxes empty.

hints: Follow the left hand arrows upwards from the elements: atomisation of Zn must give Zn(g), then atomisation of S must give S(g).
After both atoms are gaseous, the next two steps up must be first and second ionisation of zinc, each adding one electron to the gas phase.
Check that every species includes the correct state symbol and that free electrons appear on the ionisation levels to balance charge.
walkthrough:
Build the cycle from the elements upward**
The bottom level where $\Delta H_{\text{at}}\text{(Zn)}$ starts and where $\Delta H_{\text{f}}$ starts must be the elements in standard states: $\text{Zn(s)} + \text{S(s)}$. Atomising zinc gives $\text{Zn(g)} + \text{S(s)}$ on the next line up.

Atomise sulfur then ionise zinc**
The arrow labelled $\Delta H_{\text{at}}\text{(S)}$ converts $\text{S(s)}$ to $\text{S(g)}$, so the next level is $\text{Zn(g)} + \text{S(g)}$. Then IE1 removes one electron: $\text{Zn}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{S(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$. Then IE2 removes the second: $\text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{S(g)} + 2\text{e}^{-}$, which matches the top left level shown.

See how the right side closes the loop**
From that top level, EA1 adds one electron to sulfur to give $\text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{S}^{-}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$, then EA2 gives $\text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{S}^{2-}\text{(g)}$. The large $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}$ arrow then falls all the way to $\text{ZnS(s)}$, while $\Delta H_{\text{f}}$ goes directly from elements to $\text{ZnS(s)}$.

Final answer: Left hand levels from bottom to top: $\text{Zn(s)} + \text{S(s)}$, $\text{Zn(g)} + \text{S(s)}$, $\text{Zn(g)} + \text{S(g)}$, $\text{Zn}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{S(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$ linked by $\Delta H_{\text{at}}\text{(Zn)}$, $\Delta H_{\text{at}}\text{(S)}$, IE1, IE2 to reach $\text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(g)} + \text{S(g)} + 2\text{e}^{-}$.

hints: Recall whether adding an electron to a larger atom down Group 16 releases more or less energy, think about distance of the outer shell from the nucleus.
Link the change in attraction for the incoming electron to atomic radius, extra shielding and the higher principal quantum number.
walkthrough:
Picture what electron affinity means**
First electron affinity is the energy change when one electron is added to each gaseous atom: $\text{X(g)} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{X}^{-}\text{(g)}$. A more exothermic value means the nucleus pulls the incoming electron strongly. Down Group 16 the atom gets much bigger.

Explain why attraction weakens**
From S to Te an extra shell is added each step. The incoming electron enters a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner electrons. The effective attraction drops, so less energy is released when the electron is gained. Hence EA1 becomes less negative.

Final answer: First electron affinity becomes less negative / less exothermic from S to Te.
Atomic radius increases as the outer electron is added in a higher shell further from the nucleus with more shielding, so there is weaker nuclear attraction for the incoming electron.

hints: Compare the charges of $\text{O}^{2-}$ and $\text{S}^{2-}$ and then compare their sizes, both anions carry the same 2- charge.
Recall how ionic separation affects the strength of attraction between $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ and the anion in the lattice.
walkthrough:
Isolate the only difference**
Both solids contain $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ with a 2- anion, so charge is identical. The difference is size. Oxygen is in Period 2, sulfur in Period 3, so $\text{O}^{2-}$ is significantly smaller than $\text{S}^{2-}$.

Link size to lattice strength**
Lattice energy depends on attraction between oppositely charged ions. Smaller ions pack closer together, so the $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ to $\text{O}^{2-}$ distance is shorter and the attraction is stronger. More energy is released when the lattice forms, so $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}$ for ZnO is more negative.

Final answer: $\text{O}^{2-}$ is smaller than $\text{S}^{2-}$ (same charge, smaller ionic radius).
There is stronger electrostatic attraction between $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$, giving a more exothermic $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}$.

hints: Count the moles of gaseous reactants and gaseous products in step 1, solids contribute very little to entropy compared to gases.
walkthrough:
Count gas moles as a quick guide**
In step 1, $2\text{ZnS(s)} + 3\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{ZnO(s)} + 2\text{SO}_{2}\text{(g)}$. Solids are highly ordered, so focus on gas. You go from $3$ moles of gas to $2$ moles of gas. Fewer gas particles means less disorder and less ways to distribute energy, so entropy decreases and $\Delta S$ is negative.
Final answer: $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is negative because moles of gas decrease: $3$ mol $\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}$ to $2$ mol $\text{SO}_{2}\text{(g)}$.

hints: Apply $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \Sigma S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \Sigma S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$ using Table 1.1 for step 2.
walkthrough:
Substitute products minus reactants**
For $\text{ZnO(s)} + \text{C(s)} \rightarrow \text{Zn(l)} + \text{CO(g)}$:
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [S^{\ominus}(\text{Zn(l)}) + S^{\ominus}(\text{CO(g)})] - [S^{\ominus}(\text{ZnO(s)}) + S^{\ominus}(\text{C(s)})]$$
$$= (50.8 + 197.7) - (43.7 + 5.7) = +199.1 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$
The positive sign makes sense because a gas is formed from solids.
Final answer: $\Delta S^{\ominus} = 50.8 + 197.7 - 43.7 - 5.7 = +199.1 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$

hints: Write $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and convert $800^{\circ}\text{C}$ to kelvin.
Convert $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ from $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ to $\text{kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ before multiplying by T to keep units consistent with $\Delta H$.
walkthrough:
Prepare temperature and units**
$T$ must be in kelvin: $T = 800 + 273 = 1073 \text{ K}$. $\Delta S^{\ominus} = +218 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} = 0.218 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ to match $\Delta H$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Calculate and interpret**
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 733 - 1073 \times 0.218 = 733 - 233.9 = +499.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
A large positive $\Delta G$ confirms the reaction is not feasible at $800^{\circ}\text{C}$, as stated.

Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$
$= +733 - (1073 \times 0.218) = +499 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (positive, so not feasible).

hints: Recall the general Group 2 nitrate decomposition pattern: nitrate gives metal oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen.
walkthrough:
Use the familiar nitrate pattern**
Group 2 nitrates and zinc nitrate all decompose on heating to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Balance N first (2 on each side needs $2\text{NO}_{2}$), then O: left has 6 O, right has $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$ O with $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}$. The doubled form $2\text{Zn(NO}_{3})_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{ZnO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$ is also accepted.
Final answer: $\text{Zn(NO}_{3})_{2} \rightarrow \text{ZnO} + 2\text{NO}_{2} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}$

hints: State how thermal stability changes down Group 2 and how cation radius changes down the group from Table 1.2.
Link the smaller, more highly polarising cation at the top to greater distortion of the $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ ion and weakening of the N-O bond.
walkthrough:
Spot the radius trend**
Table 1.2 shows $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ 65 pm up to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ 135 pm. Larger cations are less polarising because the same 2+ charge is spread over a larger volume, so charge density falls.

Connect polarisation to decomposition**
A small highly charged cation like $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ strongly attracts the electron cloud of the nitrate ion, distorting it and weakening an N-O bond. This makes it easier to break into $\text{NO}_{2}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$. Down the group distortion decreases, more heat is needed, so stability increases.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down the group as cation radius increases.
Smaller cations cause greater polarisation / distortion of $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ and weakening of the N-O bond, so decomposition is easier at the top of the group.

hints: Compare the radius of $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ (74 pm) with each Group 2 cation and remember smaller cations give less stable nitrates.
walkthrough:
Find cations smaller than zinc**
$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is 74 pm. Only $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ at 65 pm is smaller. Since smaller means more polarising and less stable, only magnesium nitrate is less thermally stable than zinc nitrate. All others ($\text{Ca}^{2+}$, $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$) are larger and therefore more stable.
Final answer: $\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$ only
